summary: An overview of the X.500 directory standard for people not familiar with it. It compares X.500-based directory services with several other directory services. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1309 introduces the X.500 directory standard to people who had not met it. It explains how the directory is built and searched, compares it with the Internet's own lookup tools of the time, and says plainly where X.500 was strong and where it fell short.

questions: x.500 compared to other directory services
how x.500 compares to other directory systems
subtitle: A plain introduction to X.500, the standard for a global directory of people and objects.

tldr.problem: The telephone network had a directory of people, but the Internet had none: the only ways to look someone up were finger, whois and the DNS, each with its own limits and none of them searchable.
tldr.mechanism: The memo explains the X.500 standard, a distributed global directory built from entries, attributes and object classes, held in a tree and searched across the whole world with queries a user can write.
tldr.outcome: It is FYI 14, an Informational document that specifies no standard. It also lists where X.500 fell short: it was not a database, it had no output formats, and searches could be slow.

today: RFC 1309 is an Informational RFC that specifies no standard, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a 1992 introduction to the X.500 standard for readers who had not met it, written at a time when the Internet's own lookup tools were still finger, whois and the DNS, and it lists as plainly what X.500 could not do as what it could.

sections.title: Why a Directory Is Needed
sections.content:
The memo opens with the problem that made directories necessary. As industry, science and technology developed, it became increasingly likely that someone far away was trying to solve the same problems you were solving, or that someone far away held information that mattered to your research or business. The growth of the telecommunications industry, from telegraphs to telephones to computer networks, had solved the problem of being able to communicate with another person, but only on one condition: you had to know how to reach them.

Alongside that growth came directory services, and the rest of the paper looks at the models of them, the limits of the current ones, and what X.500 does about those limits. X.500 is a CCITT protocol designed to build a distributed, global directory, and the memo was produced by the Directory Information Services (pilot) Infrastructure Working Group, a joint effort of the User Services and the OSI Integration Areas of the IETF.

The memo draws the contrast with the telephone directory first. A local telephone company keeps an online list of the names of people with phone service, their numbers and their addresses, reachable by calling Directory Assistance and giving the name and address of the party, and also published in a phone book each year. The companies can offer this because they administer the pool of numbers. But the service has limits: you can find a number only if you know the name and the city or locality, and if two people in the same locality share a name there is nothing extra to tell them apart. The printed phone book can be a year out of date and the internal directory two weeks out of date. And you have to call Directory Assistance in a given area code, so one number does not work consistently everywhere. Information that businesses put in the Yellow Pages is not available through Directory Assistance at all and has to be read from the book.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the Internet, the phone company kept the list of who had which number, and you could ask it for an address if you knew a name and a town. The Internet had no equivalent. This memo describes the standard that was meant to build one.

sections.title: The Directory Services the Internet Already Had
sections.content:
The memo then looks at the lookup tools the Internet actually had, and their limits.

The finger protocol, implemented for UNIX systems and a few others, lets you ask a host about a specific person or user name, for example finger clw@mazatzal.merit.edu. The output format is not specified by the protocol. The first three lines come from the UNIX operating system's own information and the rest from a file called .plan that each user maintains. The limits are severe: you must already know which host to ask, so people on other operating systems cannot be found at all; fingerd is often switched off for security reasons; a person listed on several machines must keep the .plan files consistent; and there is no way to search the .plan files to find, say, everyone at a given site who works on X.500. The memo concludes that fingerd has limited usefulness as a piece of the Internet directory.

The whois utility queries a single centralised database maintained at the DDN Network Information Center, for many years at SRI International and now at GSI. It holds a large amount of information about the people and equipment used to build the Internet, collected as part of the Network Information Center's role, and it also holds information about the DNS, hosts, major regional networks and large parts of MILNET. The interface is simple, a query such as whois Reynolds returns a list, and a further lookup by identifier returns the full record. But a single machine has the flaws of a single machine: a processor bottleneck makes responses slow at peak times even for unrelated queries, a storage bottleneck forces the administrators to limit how much information each entry can hold, and every change has to be mailed to a hostmaster and physically retyped into the database, which slows it down and invites transcription errors.

The Domain Name System was the one that worked. Each domain is registered with the Network Information Center, and at registration a primary and perhaps some secondary nameservers are named, each of which must supply the host name to IP address mapping for that domain, so the name service is supplied in a distributed way; a domain may also be split into subdomains with a different nameserver for each. It can be queried directly with nslookup. But it was built for a narrow job, and the memo is clear about the gap: to find a given person you still need the DNS and finger together, and the DNS has very limited search capabilities. The lack of search alone shows that a rich directory service cannot be built on the DNS.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet had three ways of looking something up and each one was partial. Finger tells you about a user on one machine. Whois holds the official records about who owns what, in one central place. The DNS turns names into addresses. None of them can answer the question people actually ask, which is: who is this person and how do I reach them?

sections.title: Entries, Attributes and Object Classes
sections.content:
The information model is described through a small example. The primary construct holding information in the directory is the entry, and each entry holds information about one object, such as a person, a computer network or an organisation. An entry is built from a collection of attributes, each holding a single piece of information about the object, such as surname, telephone number or postal address. Each attribute has an attribute syntax describing the type of data it holds, for example photo data, a time code or a string of letters and numbers. So an entry for a person might carry a surname of Smith, a telephone number of 999-9999 and a title of Janitor. The syntax for the surname attribute is CaseIgnoreString, so any string is allowed and case does not matter; the syntax for the telephone number is TelephoneNumber, which allows digits, dashes, parentheses and a plus sign. The memo suggests a database analogy: a directory entry is like a database record, an attribute like a field in that record, and an attribute syntax like the field type.

At this point there is still no way to know what kind of object an entry describes, so X.500 uses the object class. Every entry contains an attribute named objectClass that says which class, or classes, it belongs to. Each object class has a definition listing the attributes that must be present and those that may be present. One class may be a subclass of another, in which case it inherits all the mandatory and optional attributes of its parent in addition to its own.

The object classes are arranged in a hierarchy by inheritance. The class called top has one mandatory attribute, objectClass, and no optional ones; every other class is a subclass of top. The class country inherits from top and adds one more mandatory attribute, c, and two optional ones, description and searchGuide. The class organization inherits from top, adds one mandatory attribute, O, and has many optional attributes. Any subclass of organization inherits everything that organization inherited from top as well as its own.

The memo points out the main benefit: it is easy to create a new class that is a slight extension of an existing one. If a class for person already holds a person's name, phone number, address and fax number, an Internet person class can be defined as a subclass of person with the additional optional attribute of e-mail address, inheriting all the person attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: An X.500 entry is a record about one thing. It is made of fields, and each field says what kind of value it holds, so a telephone number field only accepts digits and dashes. Each record also names its class, and classes can inherit fields from one another, so a new kind of record only has to state what is different.

sections.title: The Directory Tree and Distinguished Names
sections.content:
X.500 organises the namespace hierarchically in the Directory Information Base, and this hierarchical organisation is called the Directory Information Tree. Every entry occupies a position in that tree. An entry with no children is a leaf entry; an entry with children is a non-leaf node. Each entry holds one or more attributes that together make up its Relative Distinguished Name, and there is a root entry with no attributes, a special case, that forms the base of the tree. The Distinguished Name of a particular entry is the sequence of the relative distinguished names of all the entries on the path from the root to that entry.

The memo builds one step at a time. At the root the relative distinguished name is nothing and the distinguished name is empty. At the next level sit countries, with relative distinguished names such as c=us, c=gb and c=ca, giving distinguished names of {c=us} and so on. At the next level sit organisations, with relative distinguished names such as o=SRI, o=Merit and o=DEC, so an organisation under the United States has the distinguished name {c=us, o=Merit}. At the third level a person such as cn=Chris Weider gives {c=us, o=Merit, cn=Chris Weider}. Each entry in the tree carries more attributes than are shown, but only one attribute per entry was used to build its relative distinguished name, and any entry could use more than one.

X.500 also allows alias names. The entry {c=us, o=Merit, cn=Chris Weider} could be found through an alias entry such as {c=us, o=SRI, ou=FOX Project, cn=Drone 1}, which points at the first entry rather than describing a separate one.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory is a tree. Each entry is named by the chain of names on the path from the top of the tree down to it, so a person is found by country, then organisation, then their own name. An alias lets the same entry be reached by a second path.

sections.title: How the Directory Is Distributed
sections.content:
The directory model has two parts. The Directory User Agent accesses the directory on behalf of a user, and the Directory System Agent holds a particular part of the whole Directory Information Base and provides an access point to it. The entire database is distributed across the world-wide collection of Directory System Agents that make up the directory, and those agents use two techniques to make that distribution invisible: chaining and referral. The memo does not detail them, saying only that to a user the whole global directory appears to be on her desk, with the aside that if the information is on the other side of the world the desk may be a bit slow.

The standard itself lists what the design buys you. Maintenance is decentralised: each site running X.500 is responsible only for its local part of the directory, so updates can be done at once. Searching is powerful, because users can construct arbitrarily complex queries. The namespace is single and global, much like the DNS but more flexible and expandable. There is a structured information framework, which defines how information in the directory is shaped and allows local extensions. And the directory is standards-based, so applications that need directory information, such as electronic mail, automated resource locators and special-purpose directory tools, can reach information anywhere in a uniform manner, no matter where they run.
sections.plainLanguage: No one machine holds the whole directory. Every site keeps the part it is responsible for, and the pieces find each other by referral and chaining, so the user sees a single directory. That also means each site can correct its own records immediately.

sections.title: What X.500 Could Do, and Where It Fell Short
sections.content:
The memo separates three stages in the evolution of X.500: the 1988 standard, X.500 as implemented in QUIPU, and the proposed 1992 standard. QUIPU is used as the worked example because it is widely used in the United States and European directory services pilot projects and because it works well.

What the 1988 standard gave a distributed directory is an enormous potential namespace, since many hundreds of machines can hold entries, and the ability to let a local organisation administer its own data, which makes the whole directory more accurate. Within it, the directory supports arbitrarily complex searches at the level of individual attributes, and because the classes an entry belongs to are kept in the objectClass attribute, a search can also ask for a particular kind of object: one could search the c=US subtree for anyone with a last name beginning with S who also has either a fax number in the (313) area code or an e-mail address ending in umich.edu. The namespace is uniform but locally extensible, with local directories able to add new object classes, attributes and attribute types. Two kinds of security are defined for directory data: Simple Authentication, which uses passwords, and Strong Authentication, which uses cryptographic keys. Simple authentication has been widely implemented and strong authentication less so. Both are invoked when a user or process attempts a directory operation through a user agent. Local benefits are real too: the University of Michigan was providing all of its campus directory services through X.500, with user agents available for a wide range of platforms including X-Windows systems and Macintoshes.

QUIPU added two things beyond the 1988 standard. Access control lists give security for each attribute of an entry, so that an entry's information can be public, readable only by members of the organisation, and modifiable only by the owner of the entry, with detect, compare, read and modify permissions decided by the reader's group membership. Replication lets a local agent keep frequently accessed information from a foreign agent on a slave basis, with updates provided automatically from the master data, which gives alternate access points and makes searches faster by cutting network transport overhead.

The memo is equally frank about the limits. X.500 is not a general purpose database and not a database management system. It defines no standards for output formats and has no report generation. The mechanisms for the directory to contain information about itself are not yet in place, so new attributes and attribute types are distributed slowly, by hand. Searches can be slow, partly because a search across a widely distributed part of the namespace pays network transmission delays and some implementations cache partial results until everyone has reported back, and partly because some implementations are slow at searching anyway, which is sensitive to processor speed and available swap space. Most implementations also put an administrative limit on how much a single search may return: in the example given, a search that returns 1000 hits might display 20 and lose the rest, so a large search has to be run as several small ones. This was done on purpose, so that an organisation can make it hard to trawl its whole database. There is also no consensus on the ideal shape of the tree, which makes it hard to add to the existing work, and the number of RFCs on aspects of X.500 deployment is growing monthly. Despite all that, the memo concludes that X.500 is very good at what it was designed to do, which is to provide primary directory services and resource location for a wide band of information.

The 1992 standard was to formalise and standardise what QUIPU had already shown to be necessary: a formalised replication procedure, enhanced searching capacities, and formalisation of access control mechanisms including access control lists. The memo ends with where X.500 was being used: as a people directory in the United States in the White Pages Pilot Project run by PSI, and in Europe as a series of nation-wide pilots under the PARADISE Project; by the FOX Project in the United States to provide whois services for people and networks and directories of objects as disparate as NIC profiles and a pilot K-12 educators directory; for electronic mail, which was how its creators first envisioned it, with the University of Michigan giving everyone a unified address such as Chris.Weider@umich.edu and an X.500 server rerouting mail transparently to the user's real address, and with Sprint using X.500 to administer the address space of its internal X.400 mail systems. The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are discussed in section 3 of the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo praises the searching and the local control that X.500 gave, and then lists what it could not do. It was not a database, it had no way to format its output, it could not describe itself, and a large search was slow and often truncated. The 1992 standard was written to fix three of those gaps.
